articles.description:
Short answer: send each generated report from the browser directly to private object storage, keep ownership and lifecycle state in Postgres, and mint a short-lived signed download URL only after your application authorizes the customer. Use a new object key for every revision, then make deletion a database-governed state transition rather than a bucket-listing exercise.
That is the least complicated design that still gives a B2B SaaS team a defensible retention boundary. The browser moves bytes. Object storage holds bytes. Postgres decides which customer may see which report, which revision is current, and when the object must disappear.
Keep those jobs separate.

articles.description:
Short answer: poll each PDF job by its ID with exponential backoff, stop at a fixed deadline, and write the resulting terminal state to the consent record. For a healthtech service, that control loop is only one of three boundaries that matter. The other two are the signing provider's evidence boundary and the data lifecycle boundary covering region, retention, and deletion.
Do not let a request handler wait forever. A slow consent packet should become an explicit timeout that a worker can reconcile, not an eternally "in progress" row. Record the elapsed duration of every completed, failed, and timed-out job; then choose the deadline from that distribution rather than from intuition.

articles.author: Cyrus
articles.description:
When organizations decide where everyday corporate files should live and how they should be shared, two architecture patterns dominate the discussion. The first is the internal file server: a self-hosted server inside the corporate network, exposed through shared drives or SMB-based network shares, managed by the IT department. The second is the encrypted document platform: a cloud-delivered or hybrid service where documents are encrypted by default, access is governed by identity-based permissions, and sharing happens through controlled links rather than raw network paths.
Neither approach is universally superior. This article compares them across a fixed set of criteria, describes where each tends to fit, and leaves the conclusion to the reader's own environment.
Four dimensions offer a …

articles.author: mp3sss
articles.description:
Every IoT alerting system I have seen work in production has rules in it, even the ones that also have models. The rules are not a legacy artefact to be removed. They encode knowledge that models cannot learn from the data available: that the pump must not run dry, that a maintenance window suppresses alarms, that a 3σ deviation at 2 a.m. with no operator on shift should become a ticket rather than a page.
This post is about building the rule layer deliberately rather than letting it accrete.
1. Hard safety limits. A model can be wrong; an interlock must not be. temp > 120 °C → cut power belongs in deterministic code with a test, not in a neural network with a confidence score.
2. Physics and plausibility. A flow reading of 900 m³/h on a 400 m³/h line is a sensor fault, not a process anoma…
articles.title: Designing a Rule Engine That Complements Your ML Model
